abstracts_analyzed.reasoning: The abstract reports a statistically significant interaction by time-to-treatment for the effect of TXA on rebleeding (p < 0.001), but the direction is opposite to the hypothesized mechanism: benefit was observed only when TXA was started after 6 hours, not when given very early. The hypothesized mechanism predicts greater benefit when TXA is given very early (within ~1 hour) and loss/harm if given late; this study finds the (clinically small) protective effect only with late administration. Additionally, there was no effect on functional outcome and no interaction for functional outcome (p = 0.53). Note also the outcome here is rebleeding (a surrogate) in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage — a different clinical population from the CRASH-2 trauma context — which limits direct generalizability, so confidence is medium.
abstracts_analyzed.evidence_quote: Time to start of TXA modifies the effect of TXA on rebleeding rate (p < 0.001), with a clinically non-relevant reduction observed only when TXA was initiated after 6 h (absolute rate reduction 1.4%).
abstracts_analyzed.title: Impact of time to start of tranexamic acid treatment on rebleed risk and outcome in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.

abstracts_analyzed.reasoning: The abstract reports a statistically significant time-by-treatment interaction in the CRASH-3 trial subset (GCS 9–15), with larger benefit when tranexamic acid is given earlier. The authors give specific treatment effect estimates at 1 hour (ORs ~0.58–0.63) and report an interaction term whose 95% CI excludes the null (interaction 1.15, 95% CI 1.03–1.27 increasing to 1.16, 95% CI 1.05–1.28 with monitored times), and state that adjustment for measurement error had minimal impact. These findings support the mechanism that earlier TXA administration yields greater mortality benefit. However, the abstract does not provide explicit data showing no benefit or harm when TXA is given after 3 hours, nor does it address 28-day bleeding-specific mortality (it focuses on head-injury death in TBI), so the part of the mechanism claiming harm after >3 hours is not demonstrated here.
abstracts_analyzed.evidence_quote: “We model the effect of tranexamic acid on head injury death using logistic regression with a time-treatment interaction term... Using monitored times increased the time-treatment interaction term from 1.15 (95% CI 1.03, 1.27) to 1.16 (95% CI 1.05, 1.28).”

abstracts_analyzed.reasoning: The abstract reports a statistically significant reduction in 28-day mortality and lower 6-month Disability Rating Scale in the subgroup of patients with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) who received a 2-g out-of-hospital TXA bolus versus placebo or standard dosing, which is consistent with the mechanism that TXA benefits patients with ICH. However, this is a secondary subgroup analysis and the abstract does not report formal interaction tests or stratified results by TBI severity (e.g., mild-to-moderate vs unsurvivable severe) to show that the treatment effect differs across severity strata. Because the finding is a post-hoc subgroup signal (exploratory) without explicit interaction statistics or severity-specific comparisons, it supports the mechanism only weakly rather than providing definitive evidence of effect modification by presence/severity of TBI.
abstracts_analyzed.evidence_quote: Among 541 participants with ICH, 28-day mortality was lower in the 2-g TXA bolus group (17%) compared with the other two groups (1-g bolus/1-g infusion 26%, placebo 27%). The estimated adjusted difference between the 2-g bolus and placebo groups was -8·5 percentage points (95% confidence interval [CI], -15.9 to -1.0) and between the 2-g bolus and 1-g bolus/1-g infusion groups was -10.2 percentage points (95% CI, -17.6 to -2.9).
